blocks.text: 2.1.1 Class Structure and Components

One release of the billing service brought three tickets. The gateway client logs `connecting to https://null:8443`, although its host field is set two lines down. A heap dump shows the session cache of report rows holding a 50 MB PDF per row. Every scheduled retry ran with the last attempt number. Constructors are unit 2.1.2, static members 2.1.3, inheritance 2.1.4.
Initializers Run Top to Bottom, After super() and Before the Constructor Body
Predict the five lines `new Account()` prints:

Base constructor
field a
instance block
field b
constructor body

javac copies the field initializers and instance blocks, in source order, into every constructor that calls `super(...)`, explicitly or implicitly, right after that call. A constructor that starts with `this(...)` gets no copy, so they run once per object. Until its initializer runs, a field holds its default: `null`, `0` or `false` (unit 1.1.2).
Spot the Problem: A Field Read Before Its Initializer Sees Its Default
The gateway client:
Printing `new Endpoint().url`:
https://null:8443

`url` is initialized first, while `host` is still `null`. Naming `host` directly there is an `illegal forward reference`, but javac doesn't follow method calls. `port` is right because it is a *constant variable* (`final`, primitive or `String`, constant initializer), and javac inlines `8443` at every read. An initializer that calls a method is never constant.
A superclass constructor runs before all of this, so an overridden method it calls sees the same defaults:
[/null/orders]
`new OrderHandler("acme")` registered `/null/orders`, so every request for `/acme/orders` got a

items: Don't call an overridable method from a constructor or an initializer: build the routes on first use, or have the subclass pass its values to `super(...)`.

blocks.text: **Java 25 differs.** Flexible constructor bodies (JEP 513, final in Java 25) allow `this.tenant = tenant;` before `super();`, and the same handler prints `[/acme/orders]`. With `--release 21` javac rejects it.
<!-- practice 1 -->
An Inner Class's Instance Holds Its Outer Object; a Static Nested Class's Doesn't
Rows of a report are cached in the user's session, which serializes them:
We cache one row of each kind, set the `report` variable to `null`, call `System.gc()` and serialize the row (the same result in 10 runs out of 10):

inner:  report collected: false
inner:  java.io.NotSerializableException: Report
static: report collected: true
static: row serialized

An inner row is created as `report.new Row(...)`, and `price()` reads the report's `currency`. To make that work, javac gives `Row` a hidden field, `this$0`, that refers to the report. The cached row keeps the report's 50 MB reachable for the session's lifetime, and serialization follows `this$0` to the non-serializable `Report`. Making `Report` serializable would silence the exception and write the PDF into every session.

javac 21 adds the field only to an inner or anonymous class that uses its outer instance (reads its fields or calls its instance methods) or is `Serializable`; lambdas are in the Reference. A listener registered on a static registry pins its outer object the same way. Declare a nested class `static` unless each instance needs its outer object, and pass it the values it needs.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Local Classes and Lambdas Capture Copies of Effectively Final Locals
LoopVar.java:8: error: local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final

A local variable lives in the method's stack frame, which may be gone by the time the lambda runs. Java copies the value into the object: a local class that reads a local variable `region` gets a field `val$region`. If the variable could change, copy and variable would disagree, so the compiler forbids it. A one-element array satisfies the compiler:
retry 3  retry 3  retry 3

All three lambdas copied a reference to the same array, and read it after the loop. Declare a new variable in each iteration instead (`int n = attempt;`), which prints `retry 1  retry 2  retry 3`. An enhanced `for` variable is already new in each iteration.
<!-- practice 3 -->
A File Has at Most One Public Top-Level Class, and the File Is Named After It
`Invoice.java` declares `public class Invoice` and `public class TaxTable`:
Invoice.java:5: error: class TaxTable is public, should be declared in a file named TaxTable.java
With `TaxTable` package-private, `Invoice.java` compiles. `Checkout.java`, in the same package, uses `TaxTable`. `javac Checkout.java` on a clean checkout:

Checkout.java:3: error: cannot find symbol
        System.out.println(new TaxTable().apply(2000));
                               ^
  symbol:   class TaxTable
  location: class Checkout

javac finds a type it hasn't compiled by its name: it looks for `TaxTable.class` or `TaxTable.java` on the class path (here the current directory). Visibility isn't the problem: compiled together, both files build. It also compiles once an older `TaxTable.class` exists, which may be stale. Give each top-level class its own file; a helper only one class uses becomes a `private static` nested class.
<!-- practice 4 -->
Summary

items: **Initializers run top to bottom, after `super()` and before the constructor body.** A field read earlier, from a method or from a superclass constructor, holds its default; a constant variable is inlined and hides the bug.
**An inner class's instance holds its outer object.** It keeps the outer reachable and drags it into serialization; a static nested class doesn't.
**Local classes and lambdas capture copies of effectively final locals.** A shared mutable holder brings back one variable for every lambda.
**A file has at most one public top-level class.** javac finds classes by file name.

**Creating an object (Java 21):**

rows: memory with every field at its default
the constructor; if it starts with `this(...)`, that constructor first
field initializers and instance blocks, in source order
the rest of the constructor body

blocks.text: **What a nested object keeps of its outer instance (javac 21):**

rows: inner class using the outer instance
inner class not using it (static members don't count)
anonymous class in an instance method
`this$0` only if it uses the outer instance or is `Serializable`
a captured `this` only if it uses one

blocks.text: Challenges

items: Your framework's base class calls `init()` from its constructor. What do you tell the teams who override it, and what would you change in the framework?
Which inner or anonymous classes in your service outlive their outer object (listeners, cached callbacks), and which of those pin a large object?
A job captures a mutable `List` that the loop keeps filling. Is that a bug?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why Java Copies Captured Values

The JVM has no lexical nesting: inner, local and anonymous classes are separate classes, and javac gives them extra fields (`this$0`, `val$region`) for what they use from outside. Copying a value instead of sharing the variable keeps the stack frame free to go. The cost shows when lambdas must count or accumulate: they need a shared holder array, which races once they run on different threads, or an `AtomicInteger`.
